paragraphs: Learning an ordinary differential equation model from noisy observations involves two connected tasks: recovering the underlying states and estimating the parameters governing their evolution. Errors in either can interfere with the other. This paper proposes BCD-prox, a block coordinate descent proximal algorithm that addresses filtering and parameter estimation together within one optimization procedure.

The approach updates blocks of variables through proximal optimization steps. The authors also show how to use it with multistep numerical discretizations, which turn continuous differential equations into computations over discrete observations. This matters because fitting an ODE model requires both an estimation strategy and a numerical representation of the dynamics.

On tested ODE systems with up to 40 dimensions, BCD-prox improves state and parameter accuracy, reduces training time, and increases robustness to noise, initialization, and hyperparameter choices relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. The paper also establishes convergence under hypotheses that cover real systems of interest. These are complementary results: empirical improvements in the evaluated systems and a convergence guarantee subject to stated mathematical conditions.
icml-2019-a-block-coordinate-descent-pro.tldr: BCD-prox jointly filters noisy ODE observations and estimates model parameters, with conditional convergence guarantees and improved performance on tested systems.

paragraphs: The paper combines variational inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo to improve approximate Bayesian inference. Its starting point is a variational distribution, a parameterized approximation to the posterior of interest. Running a few MCMC steps improves this distribution, but incorporating that improvement into a tractable learning objective requires a different way to measure discrepancy.

The authors introduce variational contrastive divergence, or VCD, in place of the standard KL divergence used in variational inference. VCD compares the initial variational distribution with its MCMC-improved version. Asymptotically, it approaches the symmetrized KL divergence between the variational distribution and the target posterior, connecting the short-run refinement procedure to a posterior-based discrepancy.

The objective can be optimized efficiently with stochastic updates to the variational parameters. Experiments on logistic matrix factorization and variational autoencoders show better predictive performance when optimizing VCD. The contribution is therefore both an inference objective and a practical training method: MCMC refinement supplies information for learning the approximation, with predictive improvements demonstrated on these two latent-variable models.
icml-2019-a-contrastive-divergence-for-c.tldr: Variational contrastive divergence uses short MCMC refinements to train variational approximations and improves predictive performance on two latent-variable models.

paragraphs: The Weisfeiler–Lehman graph kernel represents graphs through subtree features and performs competitively on many classification tasks. However, these features do not capture connected components and cycles, which describe important aspects of graph topology. This paper extends the representation so that a classifier can use those structural properties alongside the existing subtree information.

The method uses information from propagated node labels to turn an unweighted graph into a metric graph, giving it a notion of distance. That transformation makes it possible to extract topological information using persistent homology. The resulting procedure augments the original features and is formalized as a generalization of Weisfeiler–Lehman subtree features.

The reported classification results are favorable, and the authors attribute most of the predictive improvement to including cycle information. This finding connects the added mathematical machinery to a particular source of useful structure. The approach matters because it expands what the graph representation can express while retaining its connection to an established classification method, rather than treating topology as a separate description.
icml-2019-a-persistent-weisfeiler-lehman.tldr: Adding persistent-homology features to Weisfeiler–Lehman graph representations improves classification in the reported results, mainly through cycle information.

paragraphs: This paper studies Gibbs sampling for determinantal point processes that select exactly k points, covering both discrete and continuous domains. The central question is whether this sampling procedure can be given rigorous efficiency guarantees. The analysis focuses on the chain's spectral gap, a mathematical quantity connected to how quickly the sampler approaches its target distribution.

The authors establish a spectral-gap bound with polynomial dependence on k and no dependence on domain size. For discrete processes, this yields sublinear-time sampling algorithms when polynomially many processors are available. The processor requirement is part of that result: the stated speedup relies on parallel computational resources.

For continuous processes, the paper also addresses whether the Gibbs sampler can actually be simulated efficiently. It proves this for a large family whose spectrum is not concentrated on the top k eigenvalues. Together, these results provide a rigorously analyzed class of efficient continuous k-DPP samplers. The contribution links control of the chain's convergence with conditions that make its computational steps feasible.
icml-2019-a-polynomial-time-mcmc-method-.tldr: The paper establishes domain-size-independent Gibbs-sampling bounds for k-DPPs and efficient continuous sampling under a spectral condition.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning builds representations from similar pairs and negative samples, encouraging similar examples to have larger representation inner products on average. Such methods can learn useful features without task labels. This paper develops a theoretical framework for explaining when that training objective can support later classification, rather than relying only on observed downstream success.

The framework introduces latent classes and assumes that semantically similar examples come from the same latent class. Under this model, the authors prove guarantees for the average classification task formed from a subset of those classes. The connection between pretraining pairs and downstream classes is therefore central to what the guarantees cover.

A generalization bound also shows that the learned representations can reduce the number of labeled examples needed for downstream tasks. Controlled text and image experiments support the theoretical account. The result gives a qualified explanation of label efficiency: contrastive training can help classification within the proposed latent-class framework, with guarantees about average tasks rather than every possible classification problem.
icml-2019-a-theoretical-analysis-of-cont.tldr: A latent-class framework explains how contrastive representations can improve average downstream classification and reduce labeled sample requirements.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo methods estimate quantities from random samples, and variability in those estimates can hinder estimation and optimization. Antithetic sampling addresses this by correlating samples instead of drawing them independently. Its practical difficulty is choosing a useful correlation structure, which can demand a design tailored to each application.

The paper proposes an adaptive framework that learns how to generate correlated samples. It provides both gradient-based and gradient-free training methods, allowing the sampler to be adjusted through different optimization approaches. Crucially, the underlying Monte Carlo estimator remains provably unbiased: the variance reduction does not come from systematically shifting the expected estimate away from the desired quantity.

Experiments in Bayesian inference and generative-model training demonstrate reduced variance and improved task performance with little computational overhead. These findings support learning a sampling strategy as a practical way to make antithetic methods more broadly usable. The theoretical contribution protects the estimator's expected value, while the empirical contribution shows useful reductions in fluctuation and gains in the evaluated applications.
icml-2019-adaptive-antithetic-sampling-f.tldr: Learned antithetic samplers reduce Monte Carlo variance while preserving unbiasedness, with practical gains in Bayesian inference and generative-model training.

paragraphs: In adversarial online learning, a learner repeatedly makes decisions while losses can be chosen adversarially. This paper adds another difficulty: the feedback used to learn from those decisions is noisy. It studies how that corruption changes achievable regret, the measure of accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison strategy.

The model uses binary losses and combines each loss with Bernoulli noise through an exclusive-or operation. In plain language, the noise can flip a loss bit, so the observed feedback may reverse the underlying outcome. The authors consider both a fixed noise rate and a rate that varies, making the noise process an explicit part of the learning model.

The analysis covers full-information feedback and bandit feedback, distinguishing access to losses across choices from feedback restricted to the selected choice. Its main results are tight regret bounds for the noisy adversarial setting. Tightness matters because it characterizes achievable performance together with corresponding limits, rather than supplying only a guarantee for one procedure. The contribution concerns these specified feedback and corruption models.
icml-2019-adversarial-online-learning-wi.tldr: The paper derives tight regret bounds for adversarial online learning with binary feedback corrupted by fixed-rate or variable-rate Bernoulli noise.

paragraphs: Speech synthesis and speech recognition map between text and audio in opposite directions. Both typically benefit from substantial paired data, which is scarce for low-resource languages. This paper uses their reciprocal relationship to train both systems with a few hundred paired examples plus additional unpaired speech and text.

Denoising autoencoders first develop modeling capabilities within each domain by reconstructing speech and text sequences. Dual transformation then lets each task create training pairs for the other: synthesized speech can train recognition, and recognized text can train synthesis. Bidirectional sequence modeling addresses error propagation, particularly in long sequences. A shared Transformer-based model structure brings these components together.

On LJSpeech, training uses 200 paired examples, corresponding to about 20 minutes of audio, alongside unpaired data. The reported TTS results are a 99.84% word-level intelligible rate and a mean opinion score of 2.68; ASR achieves an 11.7% phoneme error rate. These results demonstrate learning with limited alignment supervision, while preserving the important distinction that the method still uses some paired examples and extra unpaired material.
icml-2019-almost-unsupervised-text-to-sp.tldr: A unified Transformer method trains speech synthesis and recognition together using 200 paired examples plus unpaired speech and text.

paragraphs: The stochastic multi-arm bandit problem requires learning which choices give better rewards while deciding which choices to sample. This paper develops a differentially private algorithm with provable optimality. Its motivation is that the private UCB approach discussed in the abstract does not match an established lower bound on the cost of private learning.

The construction instead starts from Successive Elimination. This method repeatedly samples the remaining arms and removes an arm once it is identified as suboptimal. To make that process private, the authors develop a private stopping rule for a stream of independent, identically distributed samples. The rule returns a multiplicative approximation to the unknown distribution's mean, and its optimality is proved.

Using that component, the private Successive Elimination algorithm meets both the non-private lower bound and the privacy-related lower bound, whose stated dependence is K log(T) divided by epsilon. This connects a private mean-estimation primitive to an optimal bandit procedure. The paper also empirically compares its algorithm with private UCB, without specifying the comparison's outcome in the abstract.
icml-2019-an-optimal-private-stochastic-.tldr: An optimal private stopping rule enables a differentially private Successive Elimination bandit algorithm that meets private and non-private lower bounds.

paragraphs: A neural network's feature extractor and classifier are often optimized together. The paper identifies a possible consequence: the extractor can produce an unnecessarily complex feature distribution tailored to one particular classifier, degrading test performance. This dependence between the two components motivates a training method that reduces explicit co-adaptation.

Feature-extractor Optimization through Classifier Anonymization, or FOCA, trains the extractor using many randomly generated weak classifiers. The method therefore exposes the learned features to multiple classifiers during optimization. Its purpose is to avoid organizing the representation around the specific requirements of a single classifier, addressing the relationship between network components directly.

Under special conditions, a mathematical proposition shows that FOCA features collapse toward a point-like distribution within each class while keeping classes separable. This describes a particularly simple class structure, but the conditions are part of the result. Experiments on real data under more general conditions provide supporting evidence. Together, the theory and experiments suggest that changing how the extractor interacts with classifiers can encourage useful feature organization.
icml-2019-breaking-inter-layer-co-adapta.tldr: FOCA trains feature extractors with many random weak classifiers to reduce co-adaptation, with conditional theory and supporting real-data experiments.

paragraphs: Deep Gaussian processes can represent complicated mappings and marginal distributions. Incorporating uncorrelated variables allows them to generate non-Gaussian marginals, which matter for modeling real-world data. The paper revisits how these variables enter the model and how the resulting posterior is approximated during inference.

Earlier approaches described in the abstract add noise directly and use sparse Gaussian processes together with mean-field Gaussian posterior approximations. Additive noise attenuates the signal, while the Gaussian approximation may inaccurately represent the posterior. The proposed method instead treats noisy variables as latent covariates, incorporating them as unobserved inputs to the model.

The authors also introduce an importance-weighted variational objective that uses analytic results and offers a way to exchange additional computation for improved accuracy. Their reported results consistently favor this objective over classical variational inference, particularly in deeper models. The contribution combines a change in how uncertainty enters the model with a more accurate inference objective, and the experiments indicate that this combination works well in the evaluated settings.
icml-2019-deep-gaussian-processes-with-i.tldr: Latent noise covariates and an importance-weighted objective improve deep Gaussian process inference in reported experiments, especially for deeper models.

paragraphs: Repeatedly evaluating models on the same benchmark raises a concern: progress might partly reflect adaptation to that particular test set. This paper examines the issue by building new CIFAR-10 and ImageNet test sets while closely following the original dataset creation procedures. It then evaluates a broad range of classifiers on the fresh images.

Accuracy falls by the reported 3%–15% on CIFAR-10 and 11%–14% on ImageNet. These drops show that performance on an established test set can overstate performance on newly collected data, even when the collection process closely follows the original. The new evaluations therefore probe how well benchmark results transfer beyond the familiar test examples.

However, models with accuracy gains on the original test sets achieve even larger gains on the new sets. This preserves evidence of meaningful progress despite the lower absolute scores. The authors interpret the pattern as suggesting difficulty generalizing to slightly harder images, rather than adaptivity to reused tests, as the explanation for the drops. That causal interpretation is presented as a suggestion supported by their results.
icml-2019-do-imagenet-classifiers-genera.tldr: Fresh CIFAR-10 and ImageNet test sets lower accuracy, while preserving model progress and suggesting sensitivity to slightly harder images.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn an unknown smooth probability function when each observation is only a Bernoulli outcome at a selected point. Such a test supplies a binary result rather than the probability itself. The learning problem is to recover the underlying function from these noisy, pointwise observations.

The authors provide a scalable algorithm and analyze its posterior update rule. They prove a convergence rate toward the true probability function in L2 norm, which measures squared error across the function's domain. This gives a quantitative account of how estimation error decreases, connecting the inference procedure to a rigorous recovery guarantee.

The framework also allows test outcomes to depend on contextual features, and a modified inference engine comes with guarantees for that setting. Numerical experiments show convergence rates consistent with the theory and better handling of contextual features than the compared state-of-the-art approach. The contribution therefore extends beyond estimating a single smooth probability relationship: it also treats additional context as part of the inference problem and analyzes that extension.
icml-2019-efficient-learning-of-smooth-p.tldr: A scalable method learns smooth probability functions from binary tests, with convergence guarantees and an extension for contextual features.

paragraphs: Label errors need not occur equally often across classes. This paper studies classification when labels are corrupted at unknown, class-dependent rates. That asymmetry matters: the abstract states that ordinary k-nearest-neighbor classification is not even consistent in this setting, so additional data alone does not ensure recovery of the desired classifier.

The authors analyze the existing Robust kNN classifier under identifiability assumptions, a measure-smoothness condition on the regression function, and Tsybakov's margin condition. Under these assumptions, its rates match the minimax-optimal rates of the noise-free problem up to a logarithmic factor. Thus, the stated noise model need not worsen the fundamental rate beyond that factor when these conditions hold.

A key analytical tool is a kNN method for estimating a function's maximum. It requires substantially fewer assumptions than existing mode estimators and may also help with noise-proportion estimation or randomized optimization. The main result supplies theoretical support for an empirically successful classifier, while the auxiliary estimation method offers a potentially useful contribution beyond classification.
icml-2019-fast-rates-for-a-knn-classifie.tldr: Under identifiability, smoothness, and margin assumptions, Robust kNN nearly matches optimal noise-free rates despite unknown asymmetric label corruption.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference makes approximate Bayesian inference practical for deep models, but its optimization still needs a starting point. The paper observes that initialization has received substantial attention for ordinary deep-learning loss minimization and much less attention for variational inference. It addresses that gap with an initialization strategy designed for the Bayesian setting.

The proposed method initializes the model layer by layer using Bayesian linear models. This makes the construction of the starting state part of the inference methodology, rather than simply borrowing a scheme developed for another optimization objective. The approach specifically targets how stochastic variational inference begins, which can affect its subsequent convergence.

The authors validate the strategy on regression and classification tasks, including Bayesian deep networks and convolutional networks. In those evaluations, it converges faster and better than alternatives inspired by initialization methods for loss minimization. The finding supports treating initialization as an important design choice for scalable Bayesian learning: changing the starting configuration improves the reported optimization behavior across multiple model and task types.
icml-2019-good-initializations-of-variat.tldr: Layer-wise initialization using Bayesian linear models improves stochastic variational inference convergence in evaluated deep and convolutional networks.

paragraphs: The paper examines gradient-based methods for nonlinear control using the complexity-analysis tools of first-order optimization. Its focus is how to describe the computational work these methods require. This connects control algorithms to a language in which progress can be analyzed through repeated calls to a clearly specified computational operation.

The authors show that complexity bounds can be expressed in terms of an oracle related to dynamic programming. That oracle can be implemented through gradient back-propagation in machine-learning libraries such as PyTorch or TensorFlow. The connection matters because the operation used in the theoretical accounting is also available through familiar computational tools.

Building on this perspective, the paper proposes a regularized Gauss–Newton algorithm with worst-case complexity bounds and improved convergence behavior in practice. It also reports a publicly available PyTorch implementation. The contribution combines an analytical view of existing nonlinear-control methods with a new algorithm: the guarantees characterize worst-case computational requirements, while the practical findings concern its observed convergence behavior.
icml-2019-iterative-linearized-control-s.tldr: An oracle-based analysis of nonlinear control leads to a regularized Gauss–Newton method with worst-case bounds and improved practical convergence.

paragraphs: Submodular optimization captures diminishing returns when selecting a set of items. This paper generalizes the problem to several disjoint sets with a shared objective. The formulation can represent allocating resources among multiple agents, where both the allocation and the combined selection matter, and the union of allocated resources must satisfy a feasibility constraint.

For maximization, the authors establish approximation guarantees for practical methods, including accelerated greedy variants and distributed algorithms, over broad constraint families such as matroids and p-systems. They also give a transfer result: an alpha approximation for the corresponding single-set multilinear formulation yields an alpha times (1−1/e) approximation in the monotone multivariate case, or alpha times 0.385 in the nonmonotone case.

For minimization, the paper gives essentially optimal approximation guarantees expressed through the objective's curvature. These results expand the collection of multivariate allocation problems with provable algorithmic treatment. The importance is the connection between a more expressive joint objective and existing optimization machinery, with the quality of the resulting solutions quantified rather than assumed.
icml-2019-multivariate-submodular-optimi.tldr: Multivariate submodular optimization extends set selection to joint allocations and provides approximation guarantees for maximization and minimization.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimating a linear time-invariant dynamical system from one observed trajectory using least squares. Its goal is a finite-time account of estimation error, rather than only a statement about what happens with unlimited observations. A central challenge is covering systems with very different dynamical behavior within one analysis.

The authors handle eigenvalues distributed across stable, marginally stable, and explosive regimes, and derive sharp upper bounds for the individual cases. A systematic analysis of a self-normalized martingale difference term is the common mathematical tool. It enables error bounds that approach the lower bound up to logarithmic factors despite the different behaviors of these regimes.

The paper also shows that least squares can be statistically inconsistent under certain conditions even when the signal-to-noise ratio is high. That finding qualifies the favorable error results: strong signal alone does not ensure that this estimator succeeds. Together, the bounds and inconsistency examples clarify both the achievable accuracy of single-trajectory identification and circumstances in which least squares can fail.
icml-2019-near-optimal-finite-time-ident.tldr: Least-squares identification receives near-optimal finite-time bounds across dynamical regimes, alongside examples of inconsistency despite high signal-to-noise ratios.

paragraphs: For networks with many parameters, a mean-field description represents training through a partial differential equation. Under appropriate assumptions, the gradient-descent equation for a single-hidden-layer network converges to a global optimum. This paper asks whether changing the dynamics can accelerate that convergence while preserving the same minimizer.

The proposed change adds non-local mass transport, implemented as a stochastic process in which neurons undergo birth and death. The authors prove faster convergence in the mean-field limit for the modified dynamics. This is a statement about the limiting equation, and the mean-field setting is central to the claimed acceleration guarantee.

To connect the theory to computation, the paper develops two classes of numerical schemes that converge to the mean-field equation and can be implemented with finitely many network parameters. Two models illustrate how the acceleration mechanism works. The contribution therefore links a modified theoretical training process to implementable algorithms, while distinguishing the proved limiting behavior from the finite-network realizations used to demonstrate the idea.
icml-2019-neuron-birth-death-dynamics-ac.tldr: Stochastic neuron birth and death implements modified training dynamics with provably faster convergence in the mean-field limit.

paragraphs: This paper studies online learning in episodic, loop-free Markov decision processes with unknown transitions. The loss function may change arbitrarily between episodes, so the learner faces both uncertainty about how actions move between states and an adversarial sequence of objectives. The analysis measures cumulative performance through regret.

The proposed algorithm uses entropic regularization. The authors establish a regret bound of order L times the number of states times the square root of the product of the number of actions and episodes, with logarithmic factors suppressed. For fixed state and action spaces and episode length, the square-root dependence on episode count gives sublinear growth in the bound.

The same methodology extends the adversarial MDP model to convex performance criteria, allowing different ways to aggregate losses within an episode. It also improves previous regret bounds. The contribution thus addresses both performance and expressiveness: it provides a stronger guarantee in the stated unknown-transition setting and supports a broader class of episode-level objectives.
icml-2019-online-convex-optimization-in-.tldr: Entropic regularization yields improved regret bounds for unknown-transition adversarial MDPs and supports convex episode-level performance criteria.

paragraphs: Plug-and-play methods place denoisers inside iterative optimization algorithms such as ADMM. This allows a pretrained denoiser to act as a prior, which is useful when there is insufficient data for end-to-end training. Despite strong empirical results, establishing whether the resulting non-convex iterations converge has remained a basic theoretical challenge.

The paper proves convergence for PnP-FBS and PnP-ADMM under a particular Lipschitz condition on the denoiser. Such a condition controls how the denoiser's outputs respond to changes in its inputs. The guarantee does not require diminishing step sizes, connecting convergence to properties of the denoiser rather than to progressively smaller updates.

The authors then propose real spectral normalization, a training technique intended to make deep denoisers satisfy the required condition. Experiments validate the theory. The contribution connects an abstract convergence requirement to a concrete training procedure: the denoiser is designed with the surrounding iterative algorithm in mind. The guarantee remains conditional on the specified Lipschitz property, rather than applying to every pretrained denoiser.
icml-2019-plug-and-play-methods-provably.tldr: A Lipschitz condition guarantees convergence of two plug-and-play methods, and real spectral normalization trains denoisers to satisfy it.

paragraphs: In finite-horizon episodic reinforcement learning, the desired objective may be total undiscounted reward. Discounting makes learning focus on a shorter effective horizon, but can shift the objective away from that goal. Using a higher discount factor preserves more long-term influence, while potentially increasing the variance of value-learning targets and making training harder.

The paper introduces TD(Delta), an extension of temporal-difference learning that decomposes a value function across time scales. Its components are based on differences between value functions with smaller discount factors. This represents a longer-horizon value through a sequence of related pieces, giving the learning procedure a structured way to handle contributions associated with different horizons.

The authors analyze useful scalability and performance properties of this decomposition and report theoretical and empirical improvements over standard TD learning in certain settings. The result offers a way to organize long-horizon value estimation without simply replacing the desired horizon with a shorter one. Its improvement claims are qualified by the settings studied, rather than establishing a universal advantage for all reinforcement-learning problems.
icml-2019-separating-value-functions-acr.tldr: TD(Delta) decomposes long-horizon value functions across discount scales, improving on standard TD learning in certain theoretical and empirical settings.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning concerns the distribution of returns rather than only a single expected value. This paper offers a common framework for understanding its algorithms as recursive estimation of distributional statistics. The framework makes explicit what information an algorithm learns and how that information supports subsequent updates.

The key decomposition separates a statistical estimator from a procedure that imputes a return distribution consistent with the estimated statistics. This distinction gives the authors a way to improve analyses of existing methods and design new ones. They use it to construct EDRL, which learns expectiles of the return distribution as its chosen statistics.

The paper compares EDRL with existing methods on several Markov decision processes to illustrate aspects of the analysis. It also develops ER-DQN, a deep reinforcement-learning version evaluated on Atari-57. These evaluations accompany the conceptual and algorithmic contributions; the abstract does not claim a particular performance ranking. The central advance is a reusable account of how statistical estimation and distribution reconstruction interact in distributional learning.
icml-2019-statistics-and-samples-in-dist.tldr: A statistics-and-imputation framework unifies distributional reinforcement learning and leads to expectile-based EDRL and its deep variant ER-DQN.

paragraphs: This paper investigates when statistical tests can detect inputs manipulated by a white-box adversary, an attacker with access to the model. Its approach looks for anomalies introduced by adversarial perturbations, particularly those optimized under p-norm constraints. The goal is to identify evidence of manipulation through the model's response to the input.

The proposed statistics can be computed and calibrated by randomly corrupting inputs. Defending a model requires access only to its log-odds. This access requirement is distinct from the attacker's white-box capabilities: the detection procedure uses a particular model output to construct its tests. The authors provide both empirical justification and conditions under which the suggested statistics guarantee effective detectability.

Experiments also show that correcting predictions at test time can achieve high accuracy for the evaluated attacks. That result extends the demonstrated use beyond flagging suspicious inputs. The paper's claims nevertheless retain their stated scope: guaranteed detection depends on conditions, and successful correction is an experimental finding. The contribution is a statistical route to detection with supporting analysis and evidence.
icml-2019-the-odds-are-odd-a-statistical.tldr: Tests calibrated through random input corruption detect adversarial anomalies under stated conditions and enable accurate prediction correction in experiments.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example was included in a model's training data. This paper derives an optimal strategy under assumptions about the distribution of trained model parameters. The analysis seeks to identify which information matters for the best possible membership decision within that setting.

Under those assumptions, the optimal attack depends only on the loss function. Consequently, black-box attacks can be as effective as white-box attacks in the analyzed model. This result ties the information needed for optimal inference to loss, while preserving the dependence of the conclusion on the parameter-distribution assumptions.

Because the exact optimal strategy is intractable, the authors develop approximations that yield several usable inference methods. They also interpret existing attacks as coarser approximations to the same strategy. Their proposed attacks outperform the compared state of the art across settings ranging from logistic regression to ResNet-101 and ImageNet. The contribution combines a theoretical account of attack information with practical approximations that show empirical gains in the evaluated cases.
icml-2019-white-box-vs-black-box-bayes-o.tldr: Under parameter-distribution assumptions, optimal membership inference depends only on loss, and practical approximations improve attacks in tested settings.
